answer.why: As an insider, that name made me laugh straight away. 'Confirmed' and 'substantive' are the exact words you wait years to see on an appointment letter, and nobody outside the service would think to use them. It tells me the developer actually knows the world. 'Minister Salary' is the obvious hook and I'd probably tap it too, but it reads like clickbait, and I'd expect a cheap shot at the salary debate rather than a game about the work.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A satirical, slightly provocative game about the million-dollar ministerial pay benchmark. I'd expect it to be about chasing the top job and the money, with the politics up front and the actual public service work as a thin layer. It would get plenty of clicks and I'd be wary of getting the details wrong or being preachy. I'd worry it treats the service as a ladder to a payout and not as a place people work in.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A dry, insider game about career progression in the service: probation, confirmation, acting appointments versus substantive ones, appraisals and the slow grind through the grades. I'd expect small, painfully accurate humour about process and wording, with the political invitation as a distant possibility rather than the whole point. It might be too obscure for outsiders, but I'd be delighted to see it done well.

best_moment.what: The young officer from Y13, now my Deputy Secretary, thanked me for honest feedback. The goodwill I had banked came back as a tea invitation the next year, and it felt earned.

worst_moment.what: The General Election. My REP of 55 against the 60 needed for a single seat sent me into a GRC, and then the result card said it was never going to be about me. I lost at 48.2% with nothing I could have done differently.

skip_year.why: I did the work well and nobody saw it, and the game just said so. It was a quiet year with no real decision in it.

answer.held_back_by: Nothing much inside the service, since I topped out as Perm Sec with a clean file. What held me back was the move into politics, where the result depends on the team and the swing, not on you. My stats counted for little there.
answer.ending_fair_why: Losing a GRC contest at 48.2% is plausible and not cruel, and the card owned up that it was not about me. I would have liked to see my REP or the MPS matter more, but the outcome is believable.
answer.chase_next: The version where I stay in the service and go for the highest office a civil servant can hold, and I would skip the political tea. I want to see what the clean-file path looks like without the election gamble.
answer.play_again_why: The run was decent but long, and I have seen the main arc. I would come back later for a different path, not straight away.

tone_breaks.line: RETIRED AS Permanent Secretary AT AGE 53
tone_breaks.note: Retiring at 53 right after a failed election is odd. Perm Secs do leave around then, but the game never explained why I had to leave the service to stand.

tone_breaks.line: When you joined, your file estimated your potential at Deputy Secretary. You were not told.
tone_breaks.note: Plausible, but it reads a little like a reveal for effect. Real systems rate current estimated potential, and it is not framed this way.

answer.title_fit_why: Most of the game is about getting confirmed and moving between grades, with appraisal wording and the slow build of trust. The ministerial pay angle only shows up at the end, and I never reached it.

RACHEL GOH · THE FINAL POSITION
Lost the Ward

Forty-eight point two percent. You shook every hand in that ward and it was not enough, and it was never going to be about you anyway.

RETIRED AS Permanent Secretary
AT AGE 53
LIFETIME EARNINGS $10.6M
INTEGRITY 100

DECLASSIFIED
YOUR CEILING: When you joined, your file estimated your potential at Deputy Secretary. You were not told.
THE YEAR IT CHANGED: At 27, in The Counter, you chose "Tell them exactly why it will fail." It removed your ceiling inside the service altogether.
EXPOSURE: Your file is clean enough to be boring. In this building, that is a compliment.
LEGACY: People you trained quote you in rooms you will never enter. Two of them say you are the reason they stayed.
